Takeaways: Use springs described by damping and response, not fixed durations; Start at 100% damping and add bounce only when the gesture itself carries momentum; Things should leave the way they came in; Highlight on touch-down, commit on touch-up, and allow dragging off to cancel; Prototype interactions as live demos, not static frames
Ideas for OnCourse: Motion: Define 2-3 shared spring presets (e.g. no-bounce for taps, slight bounce for swipe-dismiss) in the design system and use them everywhere instead of ad-hoc durations. Flashcards: Make the card swipe follow the finger one-to-one and use release velocity to decide know/don't-know, so a quick flick counts. Practice: Make answer options highlight on press-in, so a learner can slide off to change their mind before committing.

Title: Explore Navigation Design for iOS (WWDC22)
Creator: Sarah McClanahan, Apple
Bottom line: Tabs should mirror your information hierarchy. Push to go deeper, and use modals only for self-contained tasks.
What they did: Using a fictional cycling app, the session shows how an overloaded first tab was split by modelling the content's natural relationships, and warns against a catch-all Home tab that duplicates actions found elsewhere. It sets rules for push (always when a chevron is shown) and modals (preferred action plus Cancel, and a sparing X).
Takeaways: Balance features across tabs instead of loading up the first one; A Home tab that duplicates functionality breaks the hierarchy (duplicating content is fine); Never switch tabs automatically, and keep each tab's state; A chevron always means push; Use X only on modals with no input, otherwise use Cancel plus a named action
Ideas for OnCourse: Navigation: Audit whether Home repeats actions that already live in Practice or Lessons, and keep Home as a launch point rather than a second copy. Practice: Present a custom test builder as a bottom modal with 'Cancel' and 'Start test', not an X, since the learner has made choices. Lessons: Use push for chapter, then topic, then lesson, with the back button showing the previous title, and keep the tab bar visible.

Title: Make Your App Visually Accessible (WWDC20)
Creator: Drew Haas, Apple
Bottom line: Never rely on color alone, design for large text from the start, and respect the system's motion and contrast settings.
What they did: An Apple accessibility engineer walks through a demo app, adding symbols to color-coded items, checking contrast (4.5:1 by default, 7.5:1 in the high-contrast variant), and switching layouts from horizontal to vertical at accessibility text sizes. He also turns off parallax and slide transitions when Reduce Motion is on.
Results: Contrast example in the demo: 4.5:1 by default ('generally the lowest acceptable ratio'), 7.5:1 in the high-contrast variant
Takeaways: Pair color with a shape or symbol for meaning (right/wrong, status); Aim for at least 4.5:1 contrast and provide high-contrast variants; Wrap text instead of truncating, and stack rows vertically at large sizes; Honour Reduce Motion by dropping idle animation, parallax and autoplay; Turn the settings on and look at your own app
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: Mark right and wrong answers with a check or cross icon as well as green and red, so color-blind learners can tell them apart. Design system: Add a contrast check (at least 4.5:1) to every text and background token pair in light and dark, and let answer rows wrap to vertical layouts at large Dynamic Type sizes. Motion: Gate celebration and confetti animations behind React Native's AccessibilityInfo.isReduceMotionEnabled.

Title: Implementing Dark Mode on iOS (WWDC19)
Creator: Kurt and Tyler, Apple UIKit team
Bottom line: Dark mode is not an inversion. Build it on semantic color names and elevation levels so screens adapt without per-mode code.
What they did: Apple's session shows converting a demo app by swapping hard-coded colors for semantic ones (system background, label, secondary label) and giving brand colors and images their own dark variants. It explains that elevated layers such as sheets get lighter backgrounds in dark mode to separate them from the black base.
Takeaways: Name colors by role (background, label, secondary label), not by value; Dark mode is subtler than inverting light mode; Elevated surfaces like sheets get lighter backgrounds in dark mode, while foreground colors stay the same; Brand colors and illustrations may need dedicated dark variants; Use four levels of text color to carry hierarchy
Ideas for OnCourse: Design system: Replace raw hex values in components with role tokens (surface/base, surface/elevated, text/primary, text/secondary) that resolve per theme. Design system: Make bottom sheets and modals use a lighter elevated surface in dark mode, not the same black as the screen behind. Lessons: Give illustrations and diagram images dark-mode variants, or put them on a light card, so they don't glare.

Title: Discoverable Design (WWDC21)
Creator: Jiabao Li and Mylène Dreyer, Apple
Bottom line: Make features obvious from the screen itself instead of explaining them in onboarding slides.
What they did: Apple designers redesign a fictional recipe app: they drop a hamburger menu for a tab bar, place features by how often they're used, label ambiguous icons, keep gestures as shortcuts next to visible buttons, and rewrite a feedback control over three rounds of testing until its consequence was clear ('Suggest toast like this').
Takeaways: People skip onboarding screens, so teach in context; Rank features and give screen space by frequency of use; Label icons that could mean several things; Gestures are invisible, so use them as shortcuts rather than replacements; Say why something was recommended ('Because you added...')
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: Replace feature-tour slides with in-context hints on the first practice session, e.g. a one-time label on the bookmark and the explanation toggle. Home: Label recommended content with its reason, e.g. 'Because you missed 4 cardiology questions'. Flashcards: Keep visible 'Again' and 'Got it' buttons even if swiping works, and make the first tap animate in the swipe direction to teach the gesture.

Title: How we redesigned the Linear UI
Creator: Linear
Bottom line: A small team redesigned the chrome in about six weeks by cutting visual noise, generating themes from three variables, and dogfooding behind a flag.
What they did: Linear refreshed its sidebar, tabs, headers and inbox, and rebuilt its themes on an LCH generator using three inputs (base, accent, contrast) instead of 98 hand-set variables per theme. That also made high-contrast themes possible. They deliberately left navigation alone and rolled the change out through a feature flag with an old/new toggle, then a private beta, then general availability.
Results: About six weeks with a small dedicated team; themes went from 98 hand-defined variables to 3 inputs; no usage metrics reported
Takeaways: Generate theme colors from a few inputs instead of hand-tuning dozens; A contrast input gives you accessibility themes almost for free; Scope tightly, since they skipped navigation because changing behavior added risk; Dogfood behind a flag with an old/new toggle; A redesign needs a dedicated team, not a side project
Ideas for OnCourse: Design system: Generate OnCourse's light and dark palettes from a small set of base, accent and contrast values so dark mode and a high-contrast mode come from the same source. Design system: Ship visual refreshes behind a PostHog flag with an internal old/new toggle before rolling out. Navigation: Keep restyling separate from navigation changes, and test each on its own.

Title: Expressive Design: Google's UX Research (Material 3 Expressive)
Creator: Google Design
Bottom line: Bolder color, shape, size and motion helped people find key actions faster, but only when basic usability stayed intact.
What they did: Over three years Google ran 46 studies with more than 18,000 participants (eye tracking, surveys, usability tests) comparing expressive designs with standard Material. In one example, the email Send button was made bigger, moved above the keyboard and given a secondary color.
Results: 46 studies, 18,000+ participants; key UI elements spotted up to 4x faster; preference for expressive designs up to 87% among 18-24-year-olds; modernity perception +34%; age gaps in fixation time largely disappeared for users 45+; scattered layouts and removing text labels hurt usability
Takeaways: Use size, color and placement to make the primary action easy to find; Put the main action near where the thumb already is; Expressiveness never beats basic function, so keep text labels; A strong minority prefers calmer designs; Test with eye tracking or timed tasks, not just preference
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: Make 'Submit' and 'Next question' larger and anchored at the bottom in the thumb zone, in a distinct color from the answer options. Home: Give the single 'Start today's plan' action clear size and color emphasis rather than equal weight with other cards. Design system: Keep text labels on icon buttons in the practice toolbar, since removing labels reduced usability in Google's tests.

Title: How Duolingo's World Characters lip sync
Creator: Jasmine Vahidsafa and Kevin Lenzo, Duolingo
Bottom line: Duolingo made characters feel alive at scale by driving Rive state machines with data, not hand-animated video.
What they did: Duolingo ran its text-to-speech audio through its own speech models to get word and phoneme timings, mapped them to 20+ mouth shapes per character, and ran mouth and body animation as parallel states in a Rive state machine. The app downloads the audio and timings and drives the animation live, so characters react to taps and to right or wrong answers.
Results: 10 characters, 40+ languages, 100+ courses, 20+ mouth shapes per character; no engagement metrics reported
Takeaways: Interactive state machines scale where hand-made video can't; Separate layers (body vs mouth) so they combine freely; Sending timing data is much lighter than shipping video; Characters reacting to right and wrong answers turn them into study buddies; Design the shapes to fit the brand before animating
Ideas for OnCourse: Motion: Use Rive (it has a React Native runtime) for any mascot or feedback animation, with states for idle, correct and incorrect driven by app events instead of Lottie clips per outcome. Practice: Add a small reacting element (icon or character) that responds to correct and incorrect answers, so feedback feels warm without extra screens.

Title: Shape language: Duolingo's art style
Creator: Megan Barker, Duolingo
Bottom line: A minimal style built from a few rounded shapes let a small team make hundreds of clear, friendly illustrations a year.
What they did: In 2018 Duolingo moved from flat, sharp, muted art on gray to bright, rounded vector illustrations on white, and the UI followed with rounded buttons. The rules: use the fewest shapes needed, exaggerate key details almost to caricature, leave white space around artwork, and angle lines toward UI elements to guide the eye.
Results: No metrics reported; the team produces 'hundreds' of illustrations a year. Qualitatively, animated skill icons held attention longer than static ones
Takeaways: Pick a style you can produce quickly with a small team; Unclear art causes wrong answers ('Our failure becomes our learners' failure'); Use playfulness to lower the fear of mistakes; Surround art with white space so it reads on small screens; Use lines and motion to point attention at UI
Ideas for OnCourse: Design system: Define a small illustration kit (2-3 base shapes, a fixed palette, a stroke rule) so devs and non-illustrators can make empty-state and milestone art that stays on style. Lessons: Keep medical diagrams minimal with exaggerated key features and generous white space so they stay legible on phones.

Title: Behind the Design: Headspace
Creator: Apple Developer (interview with Jeff Birkeland, Headspace)
Bottom line: Headspace replaced category tabs with a Today tab that offers one-tap activities by time of day, and moved the full library into Explore.
What they did: Following user research, Headspace removed core tabs for meditation, focus, movement and sleep, and made a Today tab that offers activities of varying lengths for morning, afternoon and night without showing categories. The deep catalogue moved into an Explore tab with purpose-named collections.
Results: No redesign-specific metrics; the app has 100M+ users in nearly 200 countries and won a 2023 Apple Design Award
Takeaways: Keep the surface simple and the depth one step away; Organize the first screen around when and why people use the app, not your content taxonomy; Purpose-named collections beat category names; A warm brand makes hard topics approachable
Ideas for OnCourse: Today's plan: Make the first tab a short, time-aware set of one-tap sessions (e.g. 10-minute warm-up, main block, evening review) rather than a list of subjects. Navigation: Move the full subject and system catalogue into a Browse/Explore tab so Home doesn't carry the taxonomy. Lessons: Name collections by goal ('High-yield for the last 30 days') as well as by subject.

Title: 35 years of product design wisdom from Apple, Disney, Pinterest and beyond (Bob Baxley)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Bob Baxley)
Bottom line: Write a few opinionated design tenets that settle repeat debates, and stay low-fidelity until the concept is clear, because the first realistic picture anchors everyone.
What they did: At ThoughtSpot, Baxley set three tenets every team had to memorize: documentation is a failure state; start simple and let users opt into complexity; the whole product should feel like it came from a single mind. The team worked in 'block brain diagrams' (chunky blocks, simpler than wireframes) for weeks so feedback stayed on the concept, then an agency produced high-res comps in a day from the design system. When redesigning a checkout, he ran a 'reality check' study where users went through checkout on eBay, Williams-Sonoma and Amazon, and learned that the shipping quote mattered almost as much as price.
Results: Apple's online store had "six designers for a store that ran in 30 some odd countries, 12 and a half thousand instances of the store doing billions of dollars of revenue." Once block frames were locked, the agency "could do the full high-res comps in a day."
Takeaways: Tenets are decision rules people would actually argue against, unlike 'simple, clear, beautiful'; keep it to 3 or 4 so people memorize them; delay the first realistic mockup (the 'primal mark') and get to the second, third and fourth idea; watch people use other apps, not just yours, to see what really matters to them; decide what emotion a screen should create, since visual choices like colour are not just opinion
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: write 3 OnCourse tenets that settle repeat debates (for example 'start simple, opt into complexity' for Practice filters) and check every crit against them. Design process: start new flows as block diagrams and only build an AI or Figma prototype once the concept is agreed. Design process: run a 'reality check' session where NEET-PG students use Marrow or PrepLadder to practise MCQs while we watch what they care about.

Title: Figma's CEO: Why AI makes design, craft, and quality the new moat for startups (Dylan Field)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Dylan Field)
Bottom line: Keep the simple things simple and the complex things possible, and ship a 'minimally awesome product' fast so feedback starts early.
What they did: Field reads feedback about Figma everywhere (Twitter/X, support channels) and pushes the team to dig for the root problem behind a request ('they say X but want Y or Z'). Leaders regularly revisit whole systems where 'we made all the right local decisions and yet together they're too complex'. For launches Figma uses 'quality, features, deadline, choose two': FigJam and Figma Slides shipped fast to get feedback, while Dev Mode needed many rebuilds before it clearly added value for developers. Early on he ran long user studies with designers he admired and treated them as feedback sessions, not a growth hack.
Results: Figma took "three and a half years to launch" and about five years to its first paying customer, which Field calls "way too long, don't do that." Dev Mode looks simpler than FigJam but "took at least three times as long."
Takeaways: Treat intuition as a hypothesis generator, then find data to support or kill each idea; many good local decisions can still add up to a too-complex system, so review the whole; pick two of quality, features and deadline, and never drop quality for good; concrete artifacts and examples win arguments with leaders better than abstract pitches; AI 'make design' features give you the most obvious answer, so unique craft becomes the differentiator
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: once a quarter, walk the whole app end to end and list places where separate screen decisions add up to too much (for example, how many entry points Home, Today's plan and Practice give for the same MCQ session). Practice: keep the default path to one tap ('Start today's questions') and put filters, subject choice and timed mode behind an opt-in. Design process: when a student asks for a feature in support or reviews, write down the underlying problem before designing anything.

Title: How to see like a designer: The hidden power of typography and logos (Jessica Hische)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Jessica Hische)
Bottom line: Train your eye by naming the feeling a typeface gives you and then working out why, and test every brand asset at its smallest real size first.
What they did: For the Lenny's Podcast refresh, Hische kept the colour and handwritten feel fans already knew, and designed the podcast avatar early because it was the main use; detailed versions failed when shrunk to avatar size. She scopes each round (broad look first, then weight, letter height, detail), lets clients mix and match options, and hands files over early so they can be tried in real use. For Jeni's Ice Cream she fixed a misread in the wordmark that only fresh eyes noticed.
Takeaways: Page through fonts, write the first feeling each gives (calm, exciting), then look for what they share: weight, width, spacing, rounded edges; slightly rounded corners make digital type feel softer and printed; geometric type is optically corrected, not mathematically perfect, so trust your eye over the grid; blur your eyes to judge overall cohesion and colour; make assets so simple to use that non-designers can apply them well without a long brand book
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: test icons and illustrations (streak flame, badges, app icon) at their smallest real size, such as a notification icon or tab bar, before polishing the large version. Design process: run a quick font-feeling exercise with the team, labelling candidate typefaces as calm, serious or friendly, to pick type that feels trustworthy for exam prep. Streaks: check that the streak illustration, numbers and type look like they came from the same hand, rather than an icon from a library next to custom type.

Title: Inside Linear: Building with taste, craft, and focus (Karri Saarinen)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Karri Saarinen)
Bottom line: Ship rough versions to yourselves within about a week, refine with a few opted-in customers, and save the polish pass for general release, which you check yourself by trying every state.
What they did: Linear teams put a feature into production in roughly the first week, visible only internally, then open it to a few opted-in customers (for example Vercel for roadmap changes) before polishing for general release. Before launch Saarinen tries every state himself; testing threaded comments with different message lengths showed janky animation and scrolling, so the release was pulled back until fixed. Linear runs no A/B tests and sets no feature metric goals, and relies on everyone talking to customers in shared Slack channels. During the year-long private beta they invited about 10 people a week from a survey-based waitlist, fixed what each cohort hit, then invited the next cohort.
Results: After about a month the waitlist had "maybe 4,000 people"; by June–July 2019 there were "100, 200 users on it and maybe about 10 companies." At public launch with pricing, "maybe one company didn't subscribe, but everyone else subscribed to that paid plan." On the optional pay-what-you-want slider, some paid "$28 per seat and some people pay $1."
Takeaways: Craft is fast iteration plus a final polish pass, not perfecting things upfront; let small engineer and designer teams own projects so they spot details like the macOS-style diagonal 'safe zone' for submenus; test real content lengths and edge states, not just the demo path; opinionated defaults beat flexible settings because users spend less time on the tool; invite beta users in small cohorts so each group finds new problems instead of the same bug
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: ship new screens behind a flag to the team first, then to a small opted-in student cohort, and only then do the polish pass before full release. Design process: before release, try every state with real content: long question stems, long explanations, images and empty states in Practice and Lessons. Practice: give one strong default session (for example 10 mixed MCQs from weak topics) instead of asking students to configure it.

Title: Building beautiful products with Stripe's Head of Design (Katie Dill)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Katie Dill)
Bottom line: Quality is growth: give named owners the most important user journeys, have them walk the whole journey as a user every quarter, and score it together.
What they did: Stripe picked 15 critical user journeys, each owned by an engineering, product and design leader. Every quarter they 'walk the store' end to end (from a Google search to the website, docs and dashboard), write a friction log with screenshots tagged from 'nice touch' to 'P0 bug', and give a colour score against a rubric of utility, usability, desirability and 'surprisingly great'. Scores are then calibrated in a product quality review with leaders. Dill also has designers drop screenshots or prototypes of work in progress into a shared Google Slides deck (now monthly) sent to the whole company, so overlapping work is spotted early.
Results: Stripe's research found "99% of the top e-commerce sites have errors in their checkout flow"; improving checkout quality gave "a 10.5% increase in business' revenue from an older form of checkout to a newer form of checkout." Onboarding quality fixes that made products easier to understand led to activations increasing (no figure given). A clearer invoice-status button reduced support contacts (no figure given).
Takeaways: Products get worse over time as other teams ship, so review whole journeys, not single screens; use colour scores, not numbers, so people give quick judgment calls instead of arguing over a 6 or a 7; walk the flow as a mixed trio (designer, engineer, PM), because each spots different problems; share examples where quality moved a metric so quality isn't treated as the opposite of growth; sketch the ideal '11-star' end state first, then ship toward it in steps
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: name 5 critical OnCourse journeys (install to first MCQ, daily plan to session done, broken streak to return, paywall to purchase, renewal) and have a designer, engineer and PM walk each one every quarter with a friction log and a red/yellow/green score. Onboarding: walk it starting from the Play Store listing and first notification, not just the in-app screens, to catch mismatches between what the listing promises and what the first screens show. Design process: keep a monthly shared deck of in-progress screens so Home, Practice and Paywall work doesn't drift apart.

Title: From managing people to managing AI: The leadership skills everyone needs (Julie Zhuo)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Julie Zhuo)
Bottom line: Diagnose with data, treat with design: data tells you where the problem is, but the fix still has to be designed, and working well with AI starts with a sharp definition of what success looks like.
What they did: At Sundial, Zhuo removed planned PM roles and asked engineers and designers to own product definition themselves, using AI to cover gaps like front-end work, with a specialist reviewing. Her team uses ChatGPT as a tutor: she feeds in a course curriculum and asks for a version suited to how she learns (analogies, examples), then explains concepts back so it can correct her. She treats TikTok posts, tweets and customer interviews as data alongside metrics, and argues chat-style products need new measures, such as grouping user intent with an LLM, because there are no tab clicks to count.
Takeaways: Use data to find where the problem is, then use design to solve it; you can't A/B test your way to a great product, but great designers are obsessed with understanding what users really do; choosing which metric to look at and whether +5% is good is judgment, not science; define success so precisely that an agent (or teammate) can tell pass from fail, which is what evals are for; learn new skills fast by having AI build a curriculum and then quizzing yourself by explaining back
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: before each redesign, write the PostHog finding that shows where the problem is (for example the step where onboarding drops), then explore design fixes; don't let the metric dictate the solution. Design process: when prompting AI prototyping tools, write explicit success criteria first (who the screen is for, the one action it must drive, what failure looks like). Design process: count Play Store reviews and support tickets as research data and tag them by theme alongside analytics.

Title: Mastering onboarding (Lauryn Isford)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Lauryn Isford)
Bottom line: Replace feature tooltips with a guided setup wizard that builds something real for the user, personalise by how people learn rather than by job title, and teach advanced features later.
What they did: Airtable rebuilt onboarding over 12–18 months: a 'Guided Onboarding' wizard asks simple button questions on the left (what project, what to track) while the user's workflow builds itself on the right; most old tooltips were retired. They then personalised it by learning and building style (for example database-savvy builders versus visual learners) instead of by role, and added 'The Mole', a panel that pops up from the bottom with tips as users explore, for ongoing education. The activation metric was strict: week-4 multi-user active, backed by individual week-2/week-4 retention and a 'Build' sophistication score.
Results: The wizard, The Mole and personalisation together "drove a 20% lift in activation rate for Airtable" over "about a six to eight month period"; the guided wizard was "the most impactful thing we did." One generic wizard was meant to cover "more than 90% of customers." She suggests a good activation metric is one only "five to 15%" of users reach, because it correlates more strongly with long-term retention.
Takeaways: Don't name features in onboarding ('This is automations'); show how they help the user or turn them on with one tap; don't push premium features in onboarding just because they predict payment, teach what the user needs first; segment by learning style, not job title; use a reverse trial: start everyone on full premium for a limited time, then drop to free; skip A/B tests when you're confident and the change is low risk, and use tests mainly to limit risk on big changes
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: turn setup into a guided builder where the student taps exam, exam date and weak subjects on one side and sees their Today's plan fill in live, instead of tooltips over Home. Onboarding: ask one question about how the student likes to study (questions first or lessons first) and route them to Practice or Lessons as their first session. Paywall: test a reverse trial where new students get full premium for 7 days and then drop to free, so they see what they would lose.

Title: Career frameworks, A/B testing, onboarding tips, selling to engineers (Laura Schaffer)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Laura Schaffer)
Bottom line: Onboarding questions that reassure users they are in the right place can raise conversion, and the scariest step should be tucked inside something familiar instead of being step one.
What they did: At Twilio, Schaffer A/B tested adding four signup questions (coding language or 'not a developer', product, use case) against a bare email-and-password form, expecting a drop. Later, a step-by-step onboarding checklist started with 'get a phone number', which scared developers new to telecom; in a deliberately rough test, users were sent to a docs page in their coding language with the phone number step tucked inside the code sample ('putting the pill in a hot dog'), and it converted better. The 'not a developer' answer later revealed a growing group of non-coders, which led to Quick Deploy on CodeExchange, a no-code way to get a working demo.
Results: Adding the signup questions, with no personalisation behind them, "improved conversion by 5%, just improved signups." The docs-page version of onboarding "converted better" even though it sent users away from the console (no figure given). Citing Microsoft and Netflix data, she says "80 plus percent" of experiment ideas fail.
Takeaways: Friction is not always bad: questions that match what users are already worrying about make them feel they're in the right place; find the step that feels scary (the 'bogeyman') and wrap it in familiar context; 'if it's not embarrassing, you've gone too far' for first test versions; use fake-door tests and mockups to kill weak ideas before paying for an A/B test; agree the confidence level and hypothesis before the test, and back up results with qualitative feedback
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: add 2–3 tappable questions (exam, attempt year, weakest subject) and A/B test them against the current flow, since questions that confirm the app fits the student may lift completion rather than hurt it. Practice: if the first session opens on a hard timed mock, test starting with a short untimed set from the student's strongest subject, with the timed mock coming later. Design process: when a funnel step drops, pull session recordings of that exact event from PostHog before redesigning.

Title: How to grow a subscription business (Yuriy Timen)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Yuriy Timen)
Bottom line: Mostly about acquisition channels for subscription apps. The design lesson is that onboarding for complex prosumer products almost always pays off: ask for relevant information up front and tailor the first screen, so new users don't face the whole product at once.
What they did: For complex prosumer editors (Airtable, Canva, Whimsical, InVideo), Timen pushes onboarding that gathers relevant information up front and customises the landing experience, so users are guided to what they came to do instead of being 'left to their own devices' in the full editor. Canva's first big growth loop was long-tail programmatic SEO on 'make' and 'template' keywords (for example wedding invitation templates). Grammarly leaned heavily on performance marketing and lacked built-in network effects, so referral loops were 'an uphill battle'. Laika, a premium fresh dog food subscription, still made give-one-get-one referrals work because the brand is so loved. He also treats paid search ads as a quick way to A/B test headlines and positioning.
Results: Through onboarding, earlier-stage companies "can two to four X activation rates easily"; Series B and later companies "can still probably get to 20 to 30% lift at activations." For prosumer SaaS, a healthy visit-to-free-signup rate is "in that 20 to 35% range" (40 to 50% with a narrow, strong-fit audience early on). Free-to-paid conversion: "anything under 5% is not going to work long term"; "ideally like more than 7%." Most $5 to $7 a month consumer subscriptions have LTVs that "cap out at 50 to 60 bucks." These are his benchmarks from advising, not measured experiments.
Takeaways: Onboarding is almost always a big opportunity for complex products; don't show new users the whole product at once; customer research (interviews, surveys, panels) always pays off and gives early teams focus; don't drop a tactic before giving it a fair test, and set guardrails (for example 2 to 3 creative angles and target click-through rates) for when to stop; referral loops work best with real network effects or a much-loved brand; paid ads can double as fast tests of messaging and positioning
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: ask what the student is preparing for and where they are weak, then land them on a cut-down Home with one suggested first session instead of every tab and feature at once. Paywall: track free-to-paid conversion against Timen's 5% floor and 7% target, and treat anything below it as a prompt to work on activation before pricing. Design process: run a round of student interviews before redesigning a major flow and share the findings with the whole team so everyone works from the same picture.

Title: Nickey Skarstad (Airbnb, Etsy, Shopify, Duolingo) on translating vision into goals, operationalizing product quality, second-order decisions, brainstorming, influence, and much more (Nickey Skarstad)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Nickey Skarstad)
Bottom line: Pair every growth metric with a quality metric, and don't be afraid to slow onboarding down if it gets people to their first real success faster.
What they did: At Etsy, Nickey's team owned seller onboarding and first pushed to open as many shops as fast as possible; that hurt the downstream metric of sellers getting a first sale, so they added friction that made sellers more thoughtful about their listings, which got them to a first sale faster (the quality metric was roughly 'first sale in seven days'). On Airbnb Experiences, the top-line goal was the review rate, a quality metric balanced against bookings, and the team dogfooded experiences constantly to catch bad ones. For reviews she uses three cross-functional check-ins (first principles, approach plus a technical review, ready to ship) instead of separate design and engineering reviews where feedback stays in silos, and she puts first principles and a second-order-effects line into spec templates.
Takeaways: Balance a growth metric with a quality metric that predicts long-term success; More onboarding friction can be right if it leads to an early win; Get sign-off on the problem and first principles before showing designs; Run reviews cross-functionally so design feedback isn't given in a vacuum; Treat one-way-door decisions (standards, core data models) with care and let two-way-door ones ship fast
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: measure success by 'first correct practice session within 1 day' rather than raw sign-up completion, and test adding a short exam-and-subject setup step if it gets students to a better first session. Design process: start each feature crit with a short first-principles check (what we solve for, what matters, what doesn't) before any screens, then do a second check on approach with engineering present. Design process: have the team dogfood the app daily on real NEET-PG question sets and log quality issues, the way Airbnb staff took Experiences.

Title: The full-stack PM | Anuj Rathi (Swiggy, Jupiter Money, Flipkart) (Anuj Rathi)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Anuj Rathi)
Bottom line: Design for the new user who is 'lazy, vain and selfish', and carry the exact promise that brought them in from the ad straight through onboarding.
What they did: At Swiggy, the team stopped onboarding new users with 'here is everything we do' and reframed it around 'what is in it for you', continuing the exact marketing message and promotion that triggered the download (for example the rupee offer) into the splash and onboarding, in language users understand. At Jupiter Money they treat a user who uses one product as having found value there, and introduce the next product later instead of pushing everything up front. Anuj runs 'show don't tell' reviews: a wall of every screen and touchpoint built around one concrete person (not a persona) at a specific moment, such as 11:00 with a given trigger, and about half his product reviews focus on that journey. He also asks teams to write three divergent PR/FAQs before picking and recommending one.
Takeaways: Assume new users are lazy (blow my mind fast), vain (don't make me change my habit) and selfish (what's in it for me); Continue the promise from the marketing message into the first screens; Lead with one 'hook' product and introduce others at the right moment, not all at once; Map the full journey for one specific person and moment, including waiting and failure states; Explore three divergent directions, then recommend one
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: match the first screens to the acquisition message (for example 'NEET-PG daily plan' vs 'MCQ practice') so the promise that brought the student in is the first thing they see, and save other features for later. Home: lead new users with one hook (today's plan or first practice set) and introduce flashcards and lessons only after they finish a first session. Design process: before a crit, build a 'show don't tell' wall for one concrete student (name, year, exam date, time of day, what triggered the open) and walk every screen and copy line against it; bring three divergent directions with one recommendation.

Title: How to build a high-performing growth team | Adam Fishman (Patreon, Lyft, Imperfect Foods) (Adam Fishman)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Adam Fishman)
Bottom line: Onboarding is the one screen flow 100% of users touch and when they are most motivated, so use it to deliver the brand's promise and set opinionated defaults that lead people toward what works.
What they did: At Patreon, creators connected their social accounts during onboarding; a data-science model flagged high-potential creators by audience size and engagement and sent them to a human who coached them. That human help lifted early revenue, and the team then built what the humans did into the product as 'opinionated defaults': three-tier pricing recommended (sweet spot three to five tiers, $3 or $5 entry rather than $1), with extra friction when creators tried to change those defaults, while keeping the choice. They judged onboarding changes with fast proxy metrics (speed to first patron and first $100 processed) plus qualitative sampling, instead of waiting 90 days. Adam only reworks onboarding when there is a new, hard-earned insight about users, not for redesign's sake.
Results: Connecting the right creator with a human at the right time 'would improve the first month of revenue or the second month of revenue that a creator made on the platform by 25%', learned 'through a lot of experimentation'; second-month payments were a key LTV input, so overall value improved by about the same amount. More generally, he says he has seen companies 'shift their curve outward by 10, 15, 20 percentage points' on cohort retention from onboarding and activation work.
Takeaways: Onboarding is where your brand's promise is first delivered, so keep the two in lockstep; Users are most motivated during onboarding, so you can ask more of them and learn about them; Use opinionated defaults: make the right path easy and the wrong path harder, but don't remove choice; Expect onboarding conversion to dip a little if retention rises, and judge with early proxy metrics; Learn with manual or human help first, then productize what worked
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: use opinionated defaults for study setup (for example pre-select a recommended daily MCQ target and plan length based on exam date) and add a confirm step when a student picks an unrealistic target, without blocking it. Today's plan: track an early proxy like 'completed first full day's plan within 48 hours' to judge onboarding changes instead of waiting for 30-day retention. Design process: before automating a feature, have mentors or the team hand-guide a small group of new students, note which advice works, and then design those patterns into the product.

Title: Unorthodox frameworks for growing your product, career, and impact (Bangaly Kaba)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Bangaly Kaba)
Bottom line: Most growth sits between onboarding and habit, and you find it by doing planned 'understand work' and using your own product as a brand-new or next-wave user.
What they did: At Instagram the team found new users followed mostly celebrities, then posted to no one and left after 7 to 9 months; the 'connections pivot' recommended real friends first at sign-up. They fixed 'account access churn' with one omnibox login field (email, phone or handle), an SMS prompt after two failed tries on a trusted device, and an offer to save login details at log-out. Because the sign-up flow logged only start and finish, the first job was logging all 8 steps to find the drop-offs. At Instacart, people's orders were mostly the same but reordering took 7 or 8 clicks and all-or-nothing, so they made reordering easy.
Results: Instagram teams ran '12 to 20 experiments a quarter a team' and '60 to 70% of them were positive and shippable'. Account access churn lost '10, 12 million people a year'; the fix 'helped drive 15, 20 million extra monthly active users a year'. After the connections pivot, retention 'doubled over the course of a year and a half'. Launching Instagram web 'increased Instagram's growth by 10%'. Registration conversion would drop 'by 15%' in new markets with nothing broken. At Instacart, 'after five times... 90% of your order was the same'.
Takeaways: Plan 'understand work' (logging, funnels, field visits) as real roadmap items, about 40% in a new area and 15 to 20% later; Use the product as a new user with no history, because power users see a different, better app; Watch the adjacent user: falling cohort curves can mean newer users understand the product differently, not that something broke; Early social proof matters: a first post that gets no response drives people away; Don't take away behaviour users need (logging out on shared phones), make the way back easy
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: log every step of sign-up and the first session as its own event so each drop-off can be seen, not just started vs finished. Practice: in the first sessions, give a quick visible reward (score vs peers, a right-answer explanation) so a new student's first effort gets a response rather than nothing. Design process: each designer tests key flows monthly on a fresh account as a next-wave student (first-time NEET-PG taker on a low-end Android phone, slow data) and logs what breaks.

Title: How to build your product strategy stack (Ravi Mehta)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Ravi Mehta)
Bottom line: Write strategy down with wireframes, not just words, and when data shows odd behaviour like big spenders, phone those users before you guess why.
What they did: For Tripadvisor trip planning, the strategy doc wasn't done until it had wireframes, because words alone gave everyone a different picture (for example, which 4 or 5 tabs go in the nav bar). At Tinder a small group of users spent hundreds of dollars a month on Super Likes and Boosts; the team assumed they were rich, but calls showed they were movers, salespeople or new in town who compared the cost to the cost of dating. That led to Tinder Platinum and a pricier Super Like with a note that lets you message before matching. Tinder also mostly avoided search filters to keep matching casual and surprising.
Results: A Super Like makes the recipient 'three times more likely to match with you'. 'A really significant percentage of a la carte revenue... was coming from a very small single digit percentage of users', spending '$200 or $300' against an average ARPU of '$30'. The super like with a note was priced 'much higher than we thought the pricing was going to be'.
Takeaways: A strategy is only shared when people can see it, so sketch the screens (Balsamiq or paper is enough); Product strategy stack: mission, company strategy, product strategy, roadmap, goals; fix problems from the bottom up; Whales show what users really value; talk to them, because the data's reason is often wrong; Users judge price against what they would otherwise spend, not against other apps; If you don't know what moves a metric, set a goal to learn first, not a goal to move it
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: compare the price to what students already spend on coaching (for example the fee for one coaching module or test series), not to other apps, and test that line. Design process: find the top 1 to 2% of paying or most active students in PostHog and run five phone calls to learn why they pay before redesigning Paywall or Renewal. Design process: every strategy or feature brief ships with low-fidelity wireframes of the main screens and the tab bar, so the team agrees on what goes where before building.

Title: Inside Etsy's product, growth, and marketplace evolution (Tim Holley)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Tim Holley)
Bottom line: Small, quick-to-read signals and one-line copy can move conversion a lot, and saved items plus timely pushes close the habit loop.
What they did: Etsy added one line to the cart, 'Etsy offsets carbon emissions from every delivery', and saw a big conversion lift they didn't expect. They show 'signals and nudges' (for example 'only one left', fast-reply sellers) and buyer review photos so shoppers can decide quickly among 100 million unique items. For retention they used the habit loop around Favorites: an updates feed plus push notifications when a favorited item goes on sale or is about to sell out. Teams run with five leads: product, engineering, design, insights (research and analytics) and marketing.
Results: On the cart text line: 'we just saw huge uplift that we really, really didn't expect' (no figure given). Tim agreed with the stat that '80% of experiments fail'. Lenny's intro: Etsy grew from 'around 500 million in GMV to over 13 billion in GMV' during Tim's time there.
Takeaways: Test copy: a one-line value statement can beat a big feature; Short, glanceable facts help people decide; don't bury them; Use saved or favorited items as triggers for useful notifications; Retention tests need 30, 60 or 90-day windows, not one session; Weekly written 'focus' posts keep a team clear on priorities
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: A/B test one plain line of copy that says what OnCourse stands for (for example explanations written by doctors who cleared NEET-PG) next to the buy button. Notifications: turn bookmarked or wrong-answer MCQs into triggers ('5 questions you got wrong last week are due for revision') with a link straight into Practice. Practice: show short signals on each question or set ('asked in NEET-PG 2023', '62% got this wrong') so students can quickly see why it matters.

Title: Superhuman's secret to success | Rahul Vohra (CEO and founder) (Rahul Vohra)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Rahul Vohra)
Bottom line: Design features like toys people want to play with, not points and badges, and pick one clear position (for Superhuman, speed) that every detail supports.
What they did: Superhuman designs with game-design principles (goals, emotions, toys, controls, flow) instead of gamification: its snooze 'time auto-completer' accepts playful input like '2d', 'in a fortnight and a day' or 'never' (with a shrug emoji), so people explore it for fun. For years every new user went through 1:1 concierge onboarding (about 20 onboarders at peak) before a self-serve flow was built. They tested 15 font families on printouts and chose Adelle Sans, with line length fixed at roughly 90 to 120 characters for reading speed. Price ($30/month) came from a Van Westendorp survey of about 100 early users, and roadmap came from the Sean Ellis 'very disappointed' survey, focusing on 'somewhat disappointed' users who love the main benefit.
Results: Stanford reward study he cites: children with no reward spent 17% of their time drawing, those expecting a reward spent 8%. Facebook's viral factor was 'about 0.7'; LinkedIn address-book import had a lifetime viral factor of 'about 0.4'. Companies under 40% 'very disappointed' struggled to grow. The median answer to 'starting to get expensive' was $30 per month. Write with AI is used '37 times per week' per user; AI-written emails grew 'four times' over 2024. Users get through email 'twice as fast' and save 'four hours or more every single week'; a consulting firm measured '3.3 hours per person per week'. Rahul's time on product/design went from '6 to 7%' to '60% to 70%' of his week after hiring a president.
Takeaways: Rewards can halve intrinsic motivation, so make the core action itself fun; A feature is a 'toy' if it invites playful exploration and pleasant surprises; Human-led onboarding of early users builds super fans and word of mouth; Price at the 'starting to get expensive' point if you are the premium option; Improve fit by fixing objections from 'somewhat disappointed' users who already love your main benefit
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: make a small interaction a 'toy' (for example a playful, forgiving input or a surprising answer reveal) instead of adding more points or badges. Streaks: check that rewards do not replace the joy of learning; lead with progress on mastery, keep badges secondary. Design process: run the Sean Ellis 'how would you feel if you could no longer use OnCourse?' survey and build for 'somewhat disappointed' users who value the same core benefit as fans.

Title: Pricing your AI product: Lessons from 400+ companies and 50 unicorns | Madhavan Ramanujam (Madhavan Ramanujam)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Madhavan Ramanujam)
Bottom line: Keep pricing simple enough that a customer can explain it back, tell it as a value story, and do not give away the 20% of features that drive 80% of willingness to pay.
What they did: Madhavan describes 'beautifully simple pricing': test it by asking customers to explain your pricing back to you, and frame price as value, as Superhuman did with $30/month told as 'a dollar a day' to get 'four hours of productivity back in the week'. He recommends showing options (good, better, best) so the talk moves from price to value. His '20-80 axiom' warns that the 20% of the product that drives 80% of willingness to pay is often the easiest to build and gets given away free. To stop churn, acquire the kind of customers who stay, rather than throwing offers at people who are already leaving.
Results: A founder who offered '100K plus 10% of incremental value, or 500K fixed' saw the 500K option negotiated to 400K, about '4X the deal'. About '5% of companies' are in a true outcome-based pricing model; the best recover '25 to 50%' of the value they create versus '10 to 20%' in classic SaaS. Prices for things you consume rise '3 to 5%' a year; revisit your pricing at least once every two years (about half that for AI companies).
Takeaways: If customers cannot explain your pricing back, it is not simple; Frame price as a daily value story, not a monthly cost; Show good-better-best options so buyers compare value, not just price; Do not give away the features that drive most willingness to pay; Stop churn upstream by acquiring the users who stay
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: restate the plan price as a small daily amount tied to a concrete outcome (for example, per day of NEET-PG prep), and test it against the plain total. Paywall: check which few features drive most of the willingness to pay (likely the Today's plan or the full question bank) and keep them out of the free tier. Onboarding: use the answers of users who renew to shape who onboarding targets and what it promises, so the app pulls in the users least likely to churn.

Title: Making time for what matters | Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky (Authors of Make Time, Character VC) (Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky)
Bottom line: Pick one daily 'highlight', put barriers between you and infinity-pool apps, and reflect on each day as an experiment; for product work, go from idea to tested prototype in five days.
What they did: Make Time's system has four steps: choose one daily Highlight (by urgency, satisfaction or joy), written on a sticky note and given a 60 to 90 minute block; Laser, which uses speed bumps such as deleting apps, logging out and turning on two-factor auth, because 'willpower is never going to win'; Energize; and Reflect, treating each day as an experiment with curiosity, not self-judgment. They name 'infinity pools', apps with endlessly refreshing content, and the 'busy bandwagon'. The Design Sprint, refined over hundreds of sprints at Google Ventures, goes from zero to a prototype tested with customers in five days. Jake's Google Meet side project had stalled for a year and a half until one focused week turned it into a working prototype colleagues used.
Takeaways: One meaningful highlight a day matters more than doing everything; Infinity-pool design pulls on users, so friction and defaults matter more than willpower; Write the goal down and keep it visible to create a reflection loop; Miss a day? Try again tomorrow (the 'Groundhog Day' idea); A five-day sprint to a tested prototype beats months of PRDs and pitches
Ideas for OnCourse: Today's plan: lead with one 'highlight' task for the day (one block of 60 to 90 minutes) and let students pick it by urgency or satisfaction, with the rest of the plan secondary. Notifications: make reminders point to the student's chosen highlight and avoid infinity-pool patterns like endless feeds; offer one quiet focus block with no prompts. Design process: run a five-day design sprint for one big open question (for example, the Renewal flow), ending with a clickable prototype tested with real students.

Title: How Airbnb innovates with design (Teo Connor)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Teo Connor)
Bottom line: Airbnb made the app feel alive again by adding touch, motion and personal touches, and by moving to real-code prototypes early.
What they did: Airbnb rebuilt checkout so the price and book button stay at the top, and cut four lines of legal copy to one. New users now get a short welcome tour built from a screenshot of their own screen, so it feels personal. The team added haptics, 3D icons, a confetti moment and a playful guest counter with an Easter egg, and moves from Figma to engineering prototypes in real code early. New visual elements like the 3D icons start in one product area and only join the design system once they prove themselves.
Takeaways: Put the key number and main button where they stay visible; A first-run tour should be short and use the user's own screen; Haptics and small surprises show users you care; Judge motion on a device in real code, not in Figma; Save special treatments for special moments or they stop surprising
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: replace generic tips with a short first-run tour that points at the student's own Today's plan and their real first task. Paywall: keep the price and the main button pinned and visible, and cut the fine print to one line. Design process: prototype key motion (streak celebration, answer feedback) in real code on a phone before signing it off.

Title: Make your designs memorable (Rafa Conde)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Rafa Conde)
Bottom line: Moments that make people feel something are memorable, but a forced intro video cost Retro signups, so make emotional moments easy to skip.
What they did: At Retro, Rafa built a short intro slideshow (about 7 seconds) that plays before sign-up, with a haptic on each photo. It starts fast and slows down, with street noise fading into piano, to match the message 'slow down'. Testing showed it lost signups, so the team made it easy to skip and made it respect the phone's mute switch. He shares every idea as a short, entertaining video (under 10 minutes, ideally 5) with music, humor and B-roll of a real phone in hand: 'Make an ad. Sell this idea.'
Results: Showing the intro video first 'lost like 20% or 30% of signups'. Measured at the end of onboarding, the drop was smaller ('the numbers get a little bit softer').
Takeaways: Find one motif (here: slowing down) and let haptics, sound and visuals all follow it; Anything placed before sign-up costs signups, so make it skippable; Respect the mute switch; Pitch ideas as short videos that sell, not as raw screen recordings; Keep a folder of small delightful details you notice in other apps
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: if we add an emotional intro, put it after sign-up or make it skippable with one tap, keep it under 10 seconds and respect silent mode. Design process: share new prototypes as a short narrated video of a real phone in hand, not just Figma frames. Practice: use haptics that match the pace of a session, for example a light tap per answer and a slower, deeper one when the set is done.

Title: Why Amo's Design Hits Different (Julien Martin)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Julien Martin)
Bottom line: Pick one core visual idea and let it shape the whole app, and design the feedback for every tap, not just the confetti.
What they did: At Amo, Julien's team spent about 4 months on a polished, luxury 'black gem' look, then dropped it because it felt cold and not fun. They found the core idea in animated real-person avatars, which led to a messy 'fridge collage' sticker style used across all their apps. In Bump, friends are shown on an iPod-style wheel under your thumb, and each face animates when it reaches the center. Zenly greeted users with cheeky mood messages and created gestures like the edge-zoom on the map.
Results: Julien mentions Zenly at 'like 40 million users'. No experiment results.
Takeaways: Find the one 'atom' (an avatar, a logo, an icon set) that sets the tone for the rest; Ask what reaction every button gives: a small animation, a haptic or a change on screen; Physical metaphors like a wheel or a Rolodex make browsing fun; Too much novelty confuses people, so step back when users don't get it; The test: are people still smiling after 45 days?
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: design the feedback for every tap (selecting an option, a correct answer, a wrong answer) with a small animation and a careful haptic, not only the end-of-set screen. Streaks: give the streak one strong visual idea that also appears on Home and in Notifications, instead of a generic flame. Home: try a cheeky, rotating greeting that reflects the student's real state (exam countdown, yesterday's score).

Title: What it takes to design an award-winning product (Balint Orosz)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Balint Orosz)
Bottom line: Craft tests ideas in the real product with real data, because fake data in tests gives misleading answers.
What they did: At Skyscanner, Balint showed that people testing with fake data picked the variant with $1,000 flights, which real buyers would hate, so Craft now prototypes in the real app and runs beta programs. Craft 3's Quick Add came from an old chat-style capture prototype, revived 5 days before launch and taken from Figma to an interactive build in about two days. For tasks, a beta of a flexible 'objects' feature showed users mostly built projects and tasks, so after reading thousands of comments the team rolled back four months of work and built tasks around documents. Designers own product decisions (there are no PMs) and engineers name spacing and animation values in code so designers can tweak them.
Results: Objects beta: 'like 2,000 users'; '90% of them were creating two type of object types', projects and tasks. Tasks: 'four months to figure this out and then we built it in two months'. Average user spends 'two three hours a day' in Craft.
Takeaways: Fake data and fake intent give misleading test results; Act on a new idea right away, because ideas fade; Look for why users ask for a feature (databases really meant tasks); Save delight for core moments and keep 'skip' screens plain; Be willing to roll back months of work when feedback says so
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: test Practice and Today's plan ideas with real students using their own question history in a beta build, not fake data in Figma. Practice: try a one-tap, chat-style quick capture for doubts or notes during a session, and sort them later. Onboarding: keep one-time screens (permissions, OTP) plain and save motion and personality for daily moments.

Title: Mastering the pillars of great visual design (Anthony Hobday)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Anthony Hobday)
Bottom line: Visual design follows learnable rules, and a few of them (alignment, grouping, fewer colors, careful brightness) give big gains fast.
What they did: Anthony collects the unwritten rules behind good interfaces. For color: give each palette color a different brightness so they don't clash, avoid flat black, avoid yellow, and use colors for meanings the product defines (red = delete) rather than cultural meanings. He limits himself to black, white and one color, warns that packing too much into one view causes confusion, and uses tricks like a 10% black border that works on any background and gradients with more stops so they don't go muddy. For type pairings, the easy path is copying experts (Typewolf, one foundry's paired fonts); the hard path is comparing letter by letter across about 100 pairings.
Takeaways: Colors with the same brightness clash, so vary brightness; Use color to mean things your product defines, like red for delete; Black, white and one accent makes a stronger look; Dense screens are hard to do well, so communicate more with less; Save examples you like and look at them again, because experience is mostly known patterns
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: give correct, wrong and selected states clearly different brightness, not just different hues, and keep each color's meaning the same everywhere. Home: count the accent colors on Home and Today's plan and cut back to one main accent so the key action stands out. Design process: keep a shared library of saved visual techniques and look at it during crits.

Title: Designing Snapchat and the future of music (Jack Brody)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Jack Brody)
Bottom line: Build products around what users are already working around, and let designers keep going with ideas others call bad, as long as they deeply believe in them.
What they did: At Snap, Jack saw people saving snaps to their camera roll and built Memories, whose flashbacks became a reason people still open the app every day. Snap Map came from people posting 'come hang' location snaps and deleting them once they left. Gesture-only navigation was fast for early users, but Snap went too far hiding the UI and new users struggled. At Suno, each prompt returns two songs, which shows that results vary and gives preference data to improve the model.
Results: At Snap the design team was 'about a dozen' product designers in a company of '5500 people'. No experiment results.
Takeaways: Watch what users work around: it shows the demand and where the friction is; Saved history and flashbacks build value people won't give up; Hidden, gesture-only UI is hard for new users; Showing two AI results teaches users that output varies and collects preferences; Expect about 20% of a designer's work to be outside their own area
Ideas for OnCourse: Streaks: add 'on this day' flashbacks (topics mastered, scores a month ago) so a student's history becomes a reason to come back. Practice: when showing AI explanations or generated questions, try offering two versions and record which one the student picks. Design process: look at what students do outside the app (screenshots of questions, notes in other apps) and build for that.

Title: Lessons from the founding designer at Linear (Adrien Griveau)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Adrien Griveau)
Bottom line: Early on, design on top of what is live, build with engineers from day one, and fix bugs users see before building new features.
What they did: Adrien designs by taking screenshots of the live app and changing them, instead of keeping a large design system, which he says slows small teams down. He shares a rough direction early, engineers build it, and they go back and forth on screenshots of the build. Features go first to staff, then to opt-in users, then to everyone. Every feature must work with the mouse; keyboard shortcuts are added on top, following a consistent set of rules. Bugs users hit come before new work, and every engineer does support.
Results: Adrien estimates that once a feature reaches everyone, '80 90% of the time' it already handles most cases. No experiment results.
Takeaways: What's live is the truth, so design on screenshots of it; About 80% of the work gets thrown away, so share rough ideas early; Write real copy, not lorem ipsum, because it changes the design; Release in stages: staff, then opt-in users, then everyone; Video walkthroughs help you sell your work and also expose weak spots
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: design changes on screenshots of the live OnCourse app with real student data, and treat production as the truth. Design process: release new Practice or Flashcards changes first to staff, then to a small opt-in group of students, before everyone. Flashcards: make every action work by tap first, then add swipe shortcuts on top for power users.

Title: Defining the visual language for DoorDash (Kathryn Gonzalez)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Kathryn Gonzalez)
Bottom line: Start a design system only when there is a real problem, build it from what the product already uses, and sell infrastructure work in small steps.
What they did: Kathryn was DoorDash's first designer and first front-end engineer, and every employee did deliveries to see the problems firsthand. She started the design system in 2017 when the team had about 10 front-end engineers and 8 designers, and timed its first version (tokens, buttons, modals) to the rebrand so it would get used. Components were picked from what the UI already used most (mostly modals). Later, each area (merchant, consumer, Dasher) got its own design-system partner and 'local systems', for example charts for merchants.
Results: By the middle of the year after the rebrand, 'everything on the website was using the design system'. Team size when it started: 'about 10 front-end engineers', '50 engineers overall', 'eight people' in design.
Takeaways: Pitch infrastructure as small, useful steps, not six months of system work; Tie a design system to a big moment like a rebrand to get adoption; Build components from what the product really uses; Different users need different quality: dense data for merchants, rich visuals for consumers; Code and Figma will never match fully; keep the basic tokens matched
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: before adding components, list what OnCourse screens really use most and standardize those first. Design process: tie token and component cleanup to a visible launch (a Home or Paywall redesign) so engineers adopt it. Design process: have each designer spend time with real NEET-PG students during a study day, the way DoorDash staff do deliveries.

Title: The art of designing for delight (Jenny Wen)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Jenny Wen)
Bottom line: Delight means going beyond what people expect, often in everyday high-traffic moments, not confetti on a finish screen.
What they did: For FigJam's launch, the team shipped just the basic whiteboard tools plus features unique to FigJam (cursor chat, emotes, high-fives) instead of trying to match every competitor feature. Cursor chat came from a daily build-and-try cycle with two engineers and a PM, testing each version in real meetings. Jenny starts projects by listing every open question, picks the few that unlock the rest, and explores the extremes ('how expressive?') to find the middle. She swapped Amazon's press-release exercise for writing pretend tweets reacting to features, to find what people would share.
Takeaways: Confetti on completion is now expected, so find surprising care in everyday moments; Delight can calm nerves or anticipate needs, like a good waiter; Launch with a few features only you have, not a list matching competitors; List all open questions and solve the key ones first; Measure delight through what people say and share, not A/B tests
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: instead of more celebration on the results screen, find an everyday moment to improve, such as already showing the right next set after a wrong-answer streak. Onboarding: support nervous moments (first mock test, choosing the exam date) with reassuring copy and guidance, like a supportive friend. Design process: run a 'pretend tweet' exercise where the team writes how a student would share a new feature.

Title: What makes a software product feel great (Janum Trivedi)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Janum Trivedi)
Bottom line: Netflix's whole-app motion and polish refresh was A/B tested and improved all core business metrics, which shows that how an app feels affects the business.
What they did: At Netflix, Janum and designer Ben Johnson spent about 9 months on an iOS refresh: a zoom transition from artwork to the detail page, and backgrounds colored from each title's artwork using about 200 lines of tuned color code. They tested the whole refresh together (control, full refresh, and refresh without the zoom) instead of piece by piece, so it wouldn't feel patched together. For Arc's download animation he used real physics so the arc and shadow worked from any click position. His ladder for good motion: animations you can interrupt, that keep their momentum when they change direction, that stretch at edges, and that always respond.
Results: Netflix A/B test of the iOS refresh: 'statistically significant'; 'all core business metrics are positive by a substantial margin' (no exact numbers given).
Takeaways: Feel is product quality, like speed and stability; Test a full redesign as one package, because splitting it up makes it feel patched together; Make animations interruptible and keep their momentum; Tune spring values for each case instead of forcing one standard; Good details respect habit, like iOS taking key taps before the keyboard finishes rising
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: make answer feedback and moving to the next question interruptible, so fast students can tap ahead without waiting for animations to finish. Flashcards: use springs that keep the swipe's speed so cards fly off and snap back naturally, tuned for each gesture. Design process: if we redesign Home, A/B test the whole new look together against the old one, not screen by screen.

Title: The trick to AI prototyping with your design system (Lewis Healey and Kyler Hall)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Lewis Healey and Kyler Hall)
Bottom line: AI prototypes look right when you start people from a pre-coded template of your app's shell plus short, AI-written design system instructions, not from a blank prompt.
What they did: Atlassian's design system team built Figma Make and Replit templates where the top nav and side nav are already coded, so the AI only edits the content area. They wrote a 2,000–3,000 line guidelines file (cut from a 5,000-line one) with a 'translating from Tailwind' section per component, plus 'recipes' (code blob plus instructions) for things like the Rovo chat box or dark mode. They used 'sticker sheets' and bounding-box prompts to learn what the AI's vision misses, and then taught people to upload smaller, zoomed-in screenshots. Guidelines are generated from the real component code so docs stay in sync.
Results: Starting from the coded nav template cut navigation errors from 'maybe like half of the prototypes' to 'nearly zero'; instructions alone gave about '50 60% accuracy' on one-shot screenshot recreation; people had been spending 'two or three hours' getting the nav pixel perfect.
Takeaways: Pre-code the app shell (chrome) so the AI edits instead of invents; Give AI 3 clean examples per component, not every variant, or it mixes them up; Map the generic names the AI knows (Tailwind, shadcn) to your component names; Big screenshots get truncated, so feed sections; Leaders sharing prototypes in reviews drove adoption more than training
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Build a coded OnCourse prototype template with the real tab bar, header and Practice/Lessons card components, so AI prototypes start inside the app shell. Design process: Keep a short AI guidelines file for OnCourse components with 2–3 clean examples each and a 'if you see this generic pattern, use this component' map. Design process: When recreating a screen from a screenshot, crop to one section at a time.

Title: Doing UX research with AI (Noam Segal)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Noam Segal)
Bottom line: Start research from the risk the team is worried about, turn it into a few tight learning goals, and share findings as short stories that show the user's pain, not bullet points.
What they did: Noam (research lead at Airbnb, Meta, Twitter, Wealthfront) frames research as risk reduction: ask the PM what risk the study addresses, then derive a short, limited list of learning goals. He uses an interview guide, not a script, because the value is in follow-up questions, and pilots interviews first. He builds rapport by spending 3–5 minutes asking about something in the participant's background. His stack: Sprig (in-product surveys, replays, usability tests), Dscout (diary studies) and an AI interviewer like Genway to get qualitative 'why' at scale.
Takeaways: Quant tells you what, qual tells you why; Interview guide, not script, and listen instead of planning the next question; Pilot your interviews and cut goals if you can't go deep; Use the 'pain-insight equilibrium': show the pain that led to the insight, ideally with video of a user struggling; Late-stage usability tests can still find copy and CTA fixes worth a lot
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Before any OnCourse study, write the risk (e.g. 'students quit after day 3 of Today's plan') and 3 or fewer learning goals, then check every guide question against them. Design process: Share research back as a 1-minute story with a clip of a student struggling, then the insight. Onboarding: Use an in-app survey plus session replays to find where new students drop off, then interview a few of them about why.

Title: Designing Claude Code (and what's coming next) (Meaghan Choi)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Meaghan Choi)
Bottom line: Let AI do the polish and small fixes so you spend your time on the hard part: the mental model and 'shape' of the product, and decide when polish is worth it.
What they did: Meaghan, design lead on Claude Code, uses HTML artifacts as a mini decision log: Claude pulls research and data to the top, states the goal, shows 3–4 design versions, and links to side explorations with the chosen option marked. Once an idea is mid-fidelity she has Claude rebuild it with real components and it becomes a PR. Through Claude in Slack she gets draft PRs with before/after screenshots for UI fixes, plus a weekly cleanup job. She stacks nicer PRs on top of engineers' PRs and is building an automated reviewer that asks her usual questions (who is this for, does it match the design system, does it need a name).
Results: She says 'more than half of my code is done like this now' (via Claude in Slack).
Takeaways: Know when to shape (mental model) vs execute; AI won't tell you the idea is wrong; Don't polish an experiment that tests a mental model; Make quality shared: raise the floor for engineers with automated reviews, don't gatekeep; Decide which UI must stay fixed (login, billing) and which can be adaptive; Just because you can build it doesn't mean it should ship
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: For each feature, make one HTML artifact with the goal, PostHog data, 3–4 options and the chosen one marked, and share that instead of a Figma link. Design process: Write down the questions Sainath asks in review (who is this for, which existing component, does it need a name) and turn them into an AI review step for engineers' PRs. Design process: Label each prototype 'testing the shape' or 'testing polish' so crits judge the right thing.

Title: Our AI design workflows have changed (again) (Kyle Zantos)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Kyle Zantos)
Bottom line: Use cheap HTML files from your AI agent as review tools: side-by-side options, before/after animations with sliders, and approve/deny lists that paste back into the agent.
What they did: Kyle has the agent run design audits with several skills and output one HTML doc listing every proposed change with approve/deny/discuss options and a 'copy all' button to paste back; for motion it shows current vs proposed animation. Ridd prototypes 4 layouts in HTML, dictates feedback while clicking, and repeats; he shipped a fidget-spinner hover effect in about 5 minutes after three rounds. Ridd also had Claude render every toast, dialog and error message on one HTML page with inline editing, to write all system copy together. Both now record Supercut videos talking over designs (like a handoff to an engineer) and give them to the agent with the Paper frame.
Results: Ridd says the agent's accuracy from his Supercut video feedback is '80 90%'.
Takeaways: Ask the agent for the closest representation of the real thing, with before/after; Explore wide and cheap in HTML before building the real app; Put all system messages on one page to write copy consistently; Talk over a design on video for AI handoff, same as for an engineer; Build an auto review loop so variations hit a basic bar before you see them
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Generate one HTML page with every OnCourse toast, error, empty state and notification text, edit them together, and paste the changes back. Design process: For motion work (streak flame, answer feedback in Practice), ask for before/after versions side by side with sliders for duration and easing. Design process: Record a short video walking through a Paper/Figma frame and hand it with the frame link to the coding agent.

Title: Takeaways from interviewing 100+ design teams about their process (Brian Lovin)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Brian Lovin)
Bottom line: Healthy design teams share rough work early in an open feed, say what they will do each week, and cut features nobody uses.
What they did: At Campsite, Brian's team 'calls their shot': Monday kickoff, Friday recap and a daily bullet list in Slack, plus 'radiating intent' (I'm doing this, speak up if not). They built Linear and GitHub issue creation because customers asked, moved the button out of an overflow menu when nobody used it, then deleted it, and zero people complained. He shares design updates like tweets in a feed so the team builds 'ambient awareness', which at Facebook (Pixel Cloud) helped him spot related work and duplicates. When asking for feedback he says what he wants feedback on and what he doesn't.
