Results: Issue creation: 'nobody used it… a handful' of issues even after making the button prominent; after deleting it 'zero people complained'.
Takeaways: What users ask for isn't always what they use; check usage, then cut; Say what you will get done and post it publicly; Share scrappy work in a feed so others can find and reuse it; Say what feedback you don't want; Pick the format for the audience: deck for execs, doc for PMs, prototype for engineers
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Post every rough OnCourse exploration (including discarded ones) to one shared channel, short and unpolished, so PMs and engineers see the process. Design process: When sharing for feedback, add one line on what you want comments on and one on what you don't. Home: Check PostHog usage for each Home card or entry point and remove ones almost nobody taps.

Title: Designing with a growth mindset (Kate Syuma)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Kate Syuma)
Bottom line: Onboarding is a journey to setup, aha and habit moments, not a tooltip tour; test small changes you can explain instead of big redesigns.
What they did: At Miro, Kate's growth team tested adding an animated, product-like preview to the sign-up flow to show value; users tried to interact with the visuals, got distracted and dropped at each step, so they removed it and conversion improved (she now thinks they should have tested a quieter version). They learned that big bets changing many things at once were hard to read, while small personalization changes had clear, explainable effects. She defines activation by working backwards: find retained or paying users, find the early actions they share, and keep the aha moment simple (e.g. create one piece of content). Her study of 80+ companies found most still rely on step-by-step tooltips users skip.
Results: In her research of 'more than 80 companies', 'more than 60% of companies' rely on step-by-step tooltips. Miro sign-up test: the animated preview made users drop 'on each step a little bit'; removing it 'worked way better' (no figure given).
Takeaways: Don't add distracting visuals to sign-up; Define habit moment first, then work back to aha and setup; Split big bets into small tests so you know why something worked; Personalize onboarding by user goal; Treat onboarding as weeks, including emails and push
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: Keep sign-up steps plain; don't add animated previews of Practice or Lessons inside the flow, show value right after sign-up instead. Onboarding: Define OnCourse's habit moment from retained students in PostHog (e.g. finish Today's plan X days in week 1), then design onboarding to reach the first MCQ set fast. Notifications: Plan the first 2 weeks of push and email as part of onboarding, tied to the setup, aha and habit steps.

Title: Plaid's culture of craft, tips for CRIT, and lessons from early Facebook (Christophe Tauziet)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Christophe Tauziet)
Bottom line: Craft comes from process: many from-scratch explorations, open work, varied crits, and a final polish review by the same senior panel before build.
What they did: Plaid added 'polish reviews': a fixed panel of about four senior ICs, including a content designer, nitpick every Figma file in the 24–48 hours before engineering starts (spacing, consistency, copy like noun vs verb buttons). Designers can call 'design jams' where others help explore a problem for an hour or more. Crits are 7–10 people and switch formats: traditional, silent crit (5 minutes of Figma comments to music), and no-context crit where the work must speak for itself. Christophe pushes designers to start each exploration on a blank artboard (like a Facebook designer who made 20 onboarding screens from scratch) and to share short face-on Loom videos with their opinion and doubts.
Results: Polish review panel comments per file dropped from '20 30 comments' a year earlier to 'five six seven' now. Best crit size: 'between seven and 10'.
Takeaways: Duplicate-and-tweak keeps you anchored on idea one; start from blank; Name a 'jam' ritual so asking for help is easy; Use silent and no-context crits; Ask 'why' instead of saying 'I like'; don't vote on designs; Do a last polish review before build, then own 'design debt' after launch
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Add a 24-hour polish review before handoff where the same 2 people check spacing, components and copy on every screen. Design process: Run a no-context crit on Paywall and Onboarding screens, since students won't get an explanation either. Design process: For the next new screen, make 10 versions each starting from blank before picking one.

Title: Make landing pages that convert (Erik Kennedy)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Erik Kennedy)
Bottom line: A sales page lives or dies on its headline and subheads; write them to state the main value and answer objections, and use real, ugly testimonials over polished ones.
What they did: Erik's headline rule: 'the most succinct statement of the greatest value for the greatest number of your customers', so any plausible buyer sees they are the target. Subheads should tell about 90% of the story and never be bare labels like 'Our process'. He lists likely objections up front and answers each with a matching testimonial (Clout Monster pairs 'even with no prior connections' with a customer who had none). He prefers small, contained animations (Lemonade's subtly moving hero, Formcarry's inline animated icons) over scroll-jacking, and uses tricks like frame breaks and the 'SLUB' label style (smaller, lighter, uppercase, bold). Ridd shares that on an education product, swapping raw Facebook-group screenshots for designed testimonial cards made the page convert worse, and putting the screenshots back recovered it.
Takeaways: Headline must make the reader self-identify as the target user; Subheads carry the story; make each one say something; Put the phrase that makes people say 'oh wow' in person high on the page; Pick testimonials that remove a specific doubt; raw screenshots feel more real; Small contained animations signal quality without distraction
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: Rewrite the headline as the single biggest benefit for most NEET-PG students and make each feature row a full claim, not a label. Paywall: Add testimonials that answer common objections (e.g. 'I started late', 'I'm repeating the exam') as real WhatsApp or review screenshots, not redesigned cards. Renewal: Lead with the outcome students mention most in interviews.

Title: Crafting interfaces with uncommon care (Josh Puckett)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Josh Puckett)
Bottom line: Use AI's speed to go deeper on a few essential moments, not to add scope; a personal, playful onboarding token people make themselves gets shared.
What they did: For Interface Craft's onboarding, Josh gave each buyer a library card they pick from an infinite canvas of color combos and sign themselves; people spent minutes on signatures and shared them, which made it spread. He moved from a 5-card picker (felt limited) to the canvas, and later added one 'magic' slider that changes hue, saturation and lightness at once and a Lissajous (infinity-shaped) slider that controls three graphic settings, with no labels, to invite play. Buttons morph in place (Edit name becomes Done, input auto-focuses, other content fades) instead of opening dialogs, and the card is dragged into a slot with sound, inspired by Mailbox's coin. He sketches rough interaction storyboards in Figma, pastes them as images into AI tools, and tries many versions fast.
Results: He launched January 13 and opened the library February 10, about 4 weeks later; there are '14 color combinations' on the card canvas. No conversion numbers given.
Takeaways: Let users co-create a token so it feels theirs and gets shared; Give the token a real use later, not just looks; Edit in place instead of popping dialogs; Combine several controls into one when the user just wants to play; Sketch interactions roughly and let AI build many versions
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: Let students create a personal 'exam card' (name, target exam, signature or color) and reuse it later on Streaks and the profile. Streaks: Add one tactile moment (drag, sound, haptic) when a streak milestone is claimed, kept to that single spot. Design process: Sketch interaction storyboards as grey boxes in Figma and paste them into the coding agent to try 5+ versions in an hour.

Title: How Swiggy Designs 0-1 Products (ft. Swiggy Designer)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with a Swiggy designer)
Bottom line: A small Swiggy team shipped whole new apps in one to two weeks by reusing the existing design system, generating mascots, food images and videos with AI, and still fixing every AI flaw by hand.
What they did: For Swiggy's cuisine filter images (90 to 100 cuisines), the team moved from Blender and Cinema 4D to Adobe Firefly, then ChatGPT image and Nano Banana Pro. They kept images consistent by giving a silhouette (same bowl, plate, glass, isometric angle) as a reference plus prompts like 'garnished with a single coriander leaf on top'. Snacc (Gen Z, own kitchen) took two weeks from idea to launch with one week for all design: they swapped the Swiggy primary token from orange to a fluorescent green (hex CAFE33) in a separate DLS, used a ginger cat mascot for every error and empty state, and sat next to engineers to check feasibility screen by screen. Motion is handed off as Lottie JSON through ImageKit links, or as a Jitter or After Effects video with easing and duration values, then a 'PP session' tests on a real phone to fix 2px and easing mismatches.
Results: Snacc went from idea to launch in "two weeks", with "one week to finish the whole design" including UI, animations, illustration, edge cases, error states and branding. Toing (larger, Swiggy-like flow) had "two weeks" total for design, iteration and visuals. Category images are A/B tested per user cohort and changed when they don't convert (no numbers given).
Takeaways: Reuse the design system and change only tokens (primary colour) to make a new product feel different fast; Get AI images consistent with a fixed silhouette or reference for angle, plate and shadow; Fix AI tells (extra thumb, rotating cherry, levitating hands) by hand or with negative prompts, because users spot AI slop; Error, empty, closed and out-of-city screens deserve a mascot and playful copy, not a generic icon; Hand off motion as Lottie or a video with easing and duration values, then tune it together on a real device.
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: give empty, error and offline states (no questions left, no internet, sync failed) one consistent character and warm copy instead of a generic icon. Design process: for new surfaces, fork only the colour tokens of the existing design system rather than building new components, and hand off motion as Lottie or a video with easing values plus a quick on-device tuning session with engineers.

Title: This is how a top Consumer Designer designs in Figma (John, Plaid)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with John, Plaid)
Bottom line: Keep the reasoning behind design options inside the Figma file itself, on labelled cards with pros and cons, and run an async polish review before anything ships.
What they did: Plaid's Figma files separate an 'end to end' page (static screens plus prototype, the page engineers use) and a 'polish' page from a messy 'workspace' page where designers explore freely and leave comments. Each exploration gets a title card with pros and cons, and John uses custom callout components (e.g. 'from @so-and-so, and here's why we went this way') because resolved comments lose their context; options are laid out left to right from minimal to dense, including worst-case truncation and wrapped text. Experiments live on a page per quarter, each with a card listing OKR, experiment name, description, hypothesis, effort and impact estimates and ship date, with control and variants beside it. Before handoff, a panel of designers does an async, non-blocking 'polish review' (accessibility, design-system colours, type sizes, padding, copy with the content strategist, e.g. using the international phone input), after which the work is marked ready for dev.
Takeaways: Split files into a clean handoff page (static plus prototype) and a free workspace page; Put a title and pros/cons on every option so crits start from 'strong here, weak there, what do others think?'; Record decisions in callouts on the canvas, not only in comments that disappear when resolved; Keep an experiment card per test (OKR, hypothesis, effort, impact, ship date) so cross-functional partners find one source of truth; Run an async polish review by other designers before marking ready for dev; Use a 4pt rhythm and eyeball during exploration, tighten only at the end.
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: in each Figma file, keep a 'handoff' page and a 'workspace' page, and label every Paywall or Onboarding option with a title card and pros/cons before crit. Design process: keep a per-quarter experiments page with one card per test (goal, hypothesis, effort, impact, ship date, control vs variant), and add a short async polish pass by another designer (contrast, tokens, copy) before marking ready for dev.

Title: The 2 Question Rule that makes Design Crits effective (John, Descript)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with John, Descript)
Bottom line: Crits get better when each review type has a clear scope and the room must ask two clarifying questions before anyone gives feedback.
What they did: Descript's head of design split reviews into three: a designers-only craft crit, a cross-functional review of work in progress (all of design and product, with a facilitator), and a formal go/no-go design review; crit does not count as approval. A 'crit vibes' guide, co-written with the team, coaches presenters to set the stage and the audience to lead with curiosity, and the facilitator enforces a 'two question entry fee': the group must ask two clarifying questions before feedback opens. Crit slots are filled in the Monday weekly (he sits in the silence until someone volunteers), crits are recorded and notes shared via Notion AI, and a weekly 'creator challenge' has designers make a video with the product to feel its paper cuts. For AI, the Notion hub has a vibe-coding setup guide for the monorepo, PRs and Figma Make, his personal Cursor rules to copy, and a custom ChatGPT 'UI writing GPT' trained on voice and tone guidelines that suggests button and screen copy from a screenshot.
Results: Team is "about nine" (seven IC designers plus the head of design and a lead researcher). PMs send "messages every week now saying how much they enjoyed" the cross-functional review (anecdotal).
Takeaways: Give craft crit, cross-functional review and go/no-go review separate scopes so roadmap debates stay out of UX feedback; Before feedback, the group asks two clarifying questions (two question entry fee); Book crit slots at the start of the week; Have designers use the product for a real task weekly to feel the pain; Share Cursor rules and a voice-and-tone copy GPT so every designer can prototype and write UI copy consistently; Write design principles that take a side on recurring dilemmas (e.g. novice vs pro) instead of 'seamless'.
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: in OnCourse crits, the presenter sets context first and the room must ask two clarifying questions before any feedback; keep crit separate from go/no-go sign-off. Design process: build a copy helper (a Claude project or skill) loaded with OnCourse voice and tone, and paste a screenshot of a Paywall or Notifications screen to get button and headline options. Design process: once a week, each designer does a real NEET-PG practice session in the app and logs the paper cuts they hit.

Title: How I Design at Granola (Pawin)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Pawin, Granola)
Bottom line: Block out flows in low fidelity first, then go app to Figma to code: capture the live app into Figma, edit it, paste a PNG into a Claude Code agent, and test one prototype link with A/B/C switchers on weekly user calls.
What they did: The Granola designer blocks out flows in Whimsical's wireframe mode (keyboard shortcuts for buttons, avatars) to think about content and hierarchy, because AI prototypes make you 'narrow down too early'. The app, not Figma, is the source of truth: he uses the html.to.design plugin ('capture current page') to pull the running web build into Figma as editable layers, edits there, copies the frame as a PNG and pastes it into Conductor (Claude Code agents, each in its own git worktree so parallel agents don't clash) with prompts like 'add Granola as an option to the CRM list... use this custom copy... place start of list'. Prototypes use real React components with a screen picker at the bottom and A/B/C variants per screen; he archives versions in plain language ('move this version to archive, duplicate it, call it V3') and shares one Vercel preview link with a share token. He runs four to six user calls a week (context, screen share of their setup, then click-through), includes realistic context screens like a fake payment step, and the team killed a collaborative notes feature after taking it away from internal users and finding they didn't miss it.
Results: He does "four to six user research calls in a week"; Granola's target is that "every single person should be speaking to a user once a week". Collaborative notes was removed after testing with "tens maybe hundreds of users over a multi-month period" (qualitative).
Takeaways: Start low fidelity to avoid locking into one AI-generated direction; Capture the live app into Figma (html.to.design) instead of maintaining a Figma copy of the app; Round-trip Figma to code by pasting a PNG into Claude Code, and use worktrees (Conductor) to run parallel agents safely; Build one prototype link with a screen picker and A/B/C variants, made with real components, for user calls; Test removal: take a feature away and see if anyone misses it.
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: build Paywall and Onboarding prototypes in the real React Native web build with a bottom screen picker and A/B/C variants per screen, share one preview link, and use it on weekly student calls. Design process: run separate Claude Code sessions in git worktrees (e.g. via Conductor) so several design explorations can run in parallel without overwriting each other. Onboarding: include a realistic context step (e.g. 'you just bought the plan') in test prototypes so students react in the right mindset.

Title: How I Built Pocket FM's Prototyping Playground (Harsha)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Harsha, Pocket FM)
Bottom line: Strip the real production app down to a backend-free playground on the real design system, then wrap setup, sharing, deploys and team knowledge in agent skills so any designer can prototype in code with real content.
What they did: Harsha took Pocket FM's web app (and later the native app), removed the backend, analytics and ad SDKs, and kept the real design system components as a shared 'console' repo with a gallery of every designer's demos, auto thumbnails, versions and attached code-handoff docs; demos pull real show data through documented APIs instead of lorem ipsum. Setup is a skill: an 'onboarding' skill checks the Mac, Xcode tools, Homebrew/node, GitHub access, creates a per-designer branch stored in a config file and starts the server; a 'push my work' skill commits, opens a PR to the QA branch, waits for the VPN-only deploy, returns a link and posts to a Slack channel. One CLAUDE.md (symlinked into .claude, .agents for Cursor/Codex) tells agents to use Figma terms (auto layout, frames, fill/hug, constraints), pull the latest before editing someone's demo, and 'don't over code, be calm and learning oriented'; plus skills for DialKit sliders on every demo, Agentation pin comments with a background 'watch mode' agent, a Mobbin skill that knows Pocket FM's domain, a design-system MCP to check which Figma components exist in code, motion skills (Emil Kowalski's web animation design, a motion design skill with iOS HIG curves), and simulator/phone-build skills. A 'learnings' side agent reads each chat transcript on push and appends unsaid rules (e.g. button noise defaults, 'don't render the iOS status bar from Figma') to a shared file in GitHub.
Results: First version of the playground took "less than a week"; used by "around 20 product designers" across four products (Pocket FM, UGC, writer, anime). No metric outcomes cited.
Takeaways: Build the prototype sandbox on the production design system and real content, not from scratch; treat designers as the users of the setup and replace setup docs with an onboarding skill; give every demo knobs (DialKit) so tweaks don't cost prompts or tokens; capture repeated corrections automatically as shared 'learnings'; Codex was preferred for computer use on simulators ('build it, run it on simulator, send me a recording on Slack'), with faster models for quick annotation loops
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: set up an OnCourse playground repo on the real React Native components with real question/lesson content, an onboarding skill and a 'push and give me a link' skill. Design process: add a CLAUDE.md rule to use Figma terms (auto layout, fill, hug) and a learnings file that collects repeated corrections from sessions. Practice: prototype answer-feedback and streak-celebration motion with live sliders for duration and easing before handing off.

Title: 7 Senior Designers Show How They Collect Design Inspiration (Shopify, DuckDuckGo, Webflow designers)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay, compilation)
Bottom line: To avoid 'AI slop', keep a daily habit of saving good work and, for each project, crop and highlight the exact parts of references you care about so people and coding agents know what inspired you.
What they did: A Shopify designer spends about 10 minutes most mornings bookmarking into Mobbin boards (real flows) and Pinterest (taste), uses Shopify's internal 'Studio' (an internal Dribbble), and for an AI content tool builds a FigJam mood board of Mobbin screenshots with yellow highlights on the specific element (e.g. Midjourney's control panel and gallery sorting) so crops can be handed to a code agent. A DuckDuckGo design engineer uses Mobbin's motion clips instead of screen-recording apps himself; others use Mobbin flows (search an app, open Flows, copy screens into Figma) for competitive audits of navigation, search, steppers, filters, settings and error pages, while trying real apps to feel motion. One designer notes dark mode in good apps uses a dark background with lighter cards, not black cards on gray.
Takeaways: Garbage in, garbage out: save good work daily and prune it to build taste; highlight and crop the exact part of a reference, especially before giving it to an agent; use Mobbin to check standard patterns that don't need reinvention, then decide where to deviate; try the real app for motion and feel; dark mode: dark background, lighter cards
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: keep a shared Mobbin/Pinterest board per OnCourse screen and crop plus annotate the exact element before pasting references into Claude Code or Cursor. Onboarding: before redesigning, pull 5–10 onboarding flows from Mobbin and mark which parts to copy and where OnCourse should deviate. Home: check the dark theme follows the dark background with lighter cards pattern.

Title: 12 Senior Designers Show Their Engineering Handoff Process (Figma, Firefox, Slack, Ramp, Shopify, Intercom designers)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay, compilation)
Bottom line: Good handoff explains why, every state and edge case, and motion as a storyboard, all in one clearly marked spec; teams designing in code now hand off a branch, PR or preview link instead.
What they did: Figma-based teams keep a separate 'specs' page with only 'ready for dev' sections, an overview and jobs-to-be-done at the top, states, hover/click interactions, long/short text, localization, empty and error states, odd spacing called out explicitly, accessibility screen-reader order, and dated update pages when specs change; one uses a spacing-measure component mapped to size tokens, another writes a grid of every permutation of a side panel and the functionality on-screen because PRDs drift. Firefox splits 'intended design' from what ships in release one after talking to engineering; one designer drew a motion storyboard with in-between keyframes, exact pixel math (pill expands to 343px) and fade timings. Others share a Loom walkthrough plus a live prototype link, or use Magic Patterns to get to 70% for alignment then go back to Figma for the source-of-truth specs. Shopify and Intercom designers instead save to a branch, share a live link with in-browser comments, and open a draft PR plus an experimental build that engineers fork.
Results: Intercom designer: engineers often say "Oh, great. I can use 80% of that" when handed a coded prototype PR. No measured outcomes.
Takeaways: Separate scratch work from a single 'ready for dev' spec; always include why, states, edge cases, empty/error and accessibility notes; put requirements on the design itself because other docs go stale; storyboard motion with keyframes and numbers; prototype link plus Loom gets better feedback than static mocks; in code, hand off a draft PR and preview link
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: hand off each OnCourse screen as a draft PR plus a preview build, with a short spec note covering why, every state (empty, error, loading, offline) and long Hindi/English text. Practice: write the answer reveal and next-question transition as a keyframe storyboard with timings before engineers build it. Paywall: list every permutation (trial, expired, renewal, discount) in one grid so nothing is missed.

Title: Inside Lovable's Design Team (Arthur)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Arthur, Lovable)
Bottom line: At Lovable the code base is the source of truth, designers explore wide with an agent in Paper, refine by hand, and the deliverable is a PR or a feature behind a flag, not a spec file.
What they did: Arthur has dropped Figma about 99% for Paper: he captures live production UI with the Paper Snapshot Chrome extension, asks the agent for variants (e.g. '15 variants' of a credits card), picks one and refines manually, leaves comments on the canvas and pastes the comment link to the agent (over the Paper MCP), which applies and resolves them. Lovable's Pulse design system is being mirrored in Paper as themes and tokens, but CI fails code that uses raw hex values, so explorations don't need to be perfect. Designers ship their own PRs through an internal 'Lovable on Lovable' setup: prompt plus a circled screenshot ('turn this button into custom button with plus icon to avoid confusion with close') produces a PR with before/after screenshots that an engineer approves. Crits are booked in an internal tool called Throughline with async comments on a FigJam board; he also built an internal SVG logo hub with a blur preview and a Slack bot so engineers stop asking for connector logos.
Results: Arthur has shipped "like I think 130 PRs" since joining; a small button fix went "from a problem statement to being merged" in "I would say 10 minutes"; Lovable has "over 100 connectors"; design team is "plus 20 people".
Takeaways: Make the code base the source of truth and let CI enforce tokens; feed design comments directly to the agent so crit feedback isn't retyped; use agents to go wide, then judge and refine by hand, which needs strong fundamentals; the new handoff is a draft PR or a feature flag to try; plain copy wins ('this uses credits'); design for user intent ('I want to sell stuff') rather than lists of integrations
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: let designers ship small polish PRs with a before/after screenshot and an engineer approval, and add a lint check that flags raw hex colors outside the design tokens. Design process: capture crit comments where the agent can read them (canvas comments or a markdown file) instead of FigJam stickies. Paywall: use plain cost wording like Lovable's 'this uses credits' instead of clever phrasing.

Title: Wealthsimple’s AI Native Design Process (Danny, Wealthsimple)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Danny, Wealthsimple)
Bottom line: Use a canvas tool (Claude Design, Paper) to go wide fast, then build the chosen idea in the real codebase with Claude Code in plan mode, so teammates react to a working thing and engineers get a pre-reviewed PR.
What they did: Danny lays his tools on a spectrum from explore to refine: Cosmos and Mobbin for references (often from outside finance, e.g. Suno or Spotify for 'help people find stocks'), Claude Design for throwaway high-fidelity clickable concepts, Paper plus Claude Code (via the Paper MCP) to have Claude draw five concepts on a canvas he can then edit by hand, and Conductor (a GUI over Claude Code that gives each task its own git worktree) to build in the Wealthsimple front-end monorepo. For an advanced-trading 'mode switch' he drew resting and hover states of a notch-style 'back to home' control in Figma, pasted the Figma selection links into Claude Code, and asked it to 'use the Figma MCP to read the designs of the selections below', always with plan mode on and 'use the ask user question tool to make sure you understand'. He sometimes opens a second tab to have another model review the plan before it builds. Before tagging an engineer on a PR he runs the team's shared 'do code review' skill, which starts eight subagents (dead code, performance, security, best practices) and returns review notes.
Results: Building the notch prototype in code took about the same time as Figma ('about equal'), but the time to useful feedback was 'much much faster' because people could click a link in the real app. The idea was not shipped, but the prototype let the team judge it without engineering time.
Takeaways: Always start in plan mode and spend your time reading the plan; strip out tests and instrumentation it adds to a scrappy prototype; Add 'use the ask user question tool' to prompts so the model interviews you and catches details you didn't write down; Use canvas tools for divergent, throwaway work and the real codebase when you need precise interaction or motion; Run a code-review skill on your own PR before asking engineers; hand off with a short video voice-over (before vs. proposed) plus the PR; Block a recurring morning focus slot, and talk to one real customer every week
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Add a 'review my PR' step to Sainath's Claude Code flow (a code-review skill or subagent pass) before engineers are tagged, and hand off with a Screen Studio clip plus the PR, not a Figma file. Design process: Start every prototype prompt in plan mode with 'use the ask user question tool', and paste Figma selection links (Figma MCP) for resting and active states. Practice: Prototype the MCQ answer-reveal and next-question transition in the real React Native app rather than Figma, since motion is exactly what Danny says Figma prototypes can't show.

Title: Claude Code Workflow for Design Teams (Alan and Becky, Beyond Identity)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Alan and Becky, Beyond Identity)
Bottom line: Rebuild your app as a front-end-only sandbox on the real design system, keep a short CLAUDE.md of rules learned while working, and put every design option behind an in-app switcher so stakeholders review one link.
What they did: Alan, head of design, first built an 'AI version' of the Figma design system in Claude over a weekend by asking Claude to 'walk me through every single step of building a design system from scratch that will work in AI' and pasting Figma screenshots as it asked; it produced a Storybook-like site and checked WCAG contrast. Following advice from Ryo Lu at Cursor, he then rebuilt the whole app page by page from screenshots as a sandbox with mock data; engineering was impressed and connected it to the production design system. His CLAUDE.md grew from corrections ('MUI components only', 'use the theme tokens', one chart library, one icon library, don't redraw logos as SVGs), and he later had Claude shrink it from about 1,000 lines to under 200; an 'audit design system' skill flags hard-coded colors, spacing and accessibility issues. Becky's sandbox includes admin and end-user views, sign-up, and even a simulated terminal using real code, plus a hidden control panel with dropdowns for option, variant, state (empty or filled) and placement; reviewers pull her branch and leave pinned comments through a VS Code plugin Alan built.
Takeaways: A sandbox rebuild lets designers explore without touching production, and option changes stay local, not global; Write CLAUDE.md rules as you hit problems, then ask Claude to tighten it for the next designer; Make a skill only for something you'll repeat, not a list of a thousand generic skills; Put options and states behind a switcher in one URL instead of 15 prototype links; Use color only where it means something (alerts in red) and show trends with weight and brightness
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Add a dev-only 'design switcher' overlay to the React Native app that flips between options and states (empty, filled, error, new user vs. returning) so crits and PMs review one build. Design process: Keep OnCourse's CLAUDE.md as a short list of rules learned from real mistakes (existing components only, theme tokens, one icon set), and add an audit skill that flags hard-coded colors and spacing before handoff. Home: Show the main number large and the change from last week small and muted, and keep red only for things that need action today, the way Becky treated her dashboard cards.

Title: 7 Top Designers Show How They Do Design Critiques (Figma, Slack, Ramp, CNN, Firefox, Hex designers)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay, compilation)
Bottom line: Good crits are set up by the presenter: state the goal, the phase and the exact feedback you want, collect feedback silently in writing, then discuss, and replay what changed last time.
What they did: A Figma designer structures crit files as context slides (goal, research, hypothesis, timeline, a 'what I need today' slide), then explorations with full-page layouts beside them, then an appendix; the crit is 30 minutes, 15–20 presenting while people drop comment pins silently, then she speed-reads the comments and sums up themes aloud; she also adds a 'riff zone', a disclaimer slide for wild ideas, and a summary of feedback acted on last time. Hex runs a weekly hour in FigJam: 2–3 minutes of context, a 5–6 minute timer for silent stickies under 'what resonates, why' and 'what could be better, why', then the presenter leads discussion. Another team's leader split reviews into craft crit, cross-functional review and go/no-go design review, wrote 'crit vibes', and requires a 'two question entry fee' where the audience asks two clarifying questions before any opinions. CNN's Jennifer demos Cursor prototypes with a version switcher and deploys each git branch to its own URL using a Cursor command ('setup multi-branch deployment'); Slack runs crits as a Slack thread with a feedback legend and a moderator who reads questions back; Ramp gathers async feedback on coded prototypes, then moves to Figma for the 'craft portion'.
Takeaways: Put 'what feedback I need today' (and what not) on a frame people can see the whole time; Silent written feedback first, then talk, so louder people don't dominate; Make the audience ask two clarifying questions before giving opinions; Open each crit with what changed since last time so people see their feedback was used; Keep crit, cross-functional review and go/no-go sign-off as separate meetings
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Start each OnCourse crit with a 'what I need today' frame and a short 'changed since last crit' list, then a 5-minute silent comment round before any discussion. Design process: Adopt the two-question entry fee and a separate go/no-go review, so crit stays about whether the UX works. Design process: Deploy each prototype branch (e.g. Paywall or Onboarding variants) to its own preview URL so reviewers comment async on the real build.

Title: Agentic Design Process at Mercury (Carol, Mercury)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Carol, Mercury)
Bottom line: When designing an AI assistant, prototype with the real model and system prompt as early as possible, link answers straight into the right screen, and make anything with real consequences need an explicit tap to confirm.
What they did: Carol designed Mercury's 'Command', an agent that lets users start from intent ('compare this month to last month') instead of the sidebar; answers link into the real page with filters set or the transaction open, and the links are generated by the back end so the model can't invent them. She sketched the mental model in Figma, then vibe-coded a chat prototype in Cursor because turn-by-turn chat can't be felt in Figma; a deterministic prototype hit a ceiling, so she paired with her PM on one wired to a real model and system prompt, and concluded 'the system prompt in a way is the product' and the team should work in prod. For money movement the agent first asks follow-up questions in plain text, then shows a draft object labelled 'Draft' with edit, cancel and send buttons, because real money must be confirmed deterministically. Thinking states were cut from a full stream of chain of thought to a single line ('searching for card data') that users can expand, after people found plain 'thinking' felt slow and the full stream too much.
Takeaways: Prototype AI features against the real model and prompt; fake deterministic answers hide the hard part; Link answers to the exact screen and filter instead of only describing data; Use buttons, not chat, to confirm actions that matter, and label object state (draft, created) clearly; Show progress as one changing line with an option to expand; Every shipped feature also goes live in a public demo environment, and craft crit checks things like matching type weights
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: If OnCourse adds an AI 'ask about my prep' box, have answers deep-link into the exact Practice set, weak topic or Lesson with filters applied, generated from app data rather than by the model. Today's plan: When an assistant changes the plan (e.g. reschedules mocks), show it as a labelled draft with Edit, Cancel and Confirm buttons before it's applied. Design process: Prototype any AI tutor or explanation feature against the real model and system prompt, not canned replies, and use a single-line expandable 'thinking' state.

Title: How I use Claude Code as a Designer at Shopify (Caston)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Caston, Shopify)
Bottom line: Diverge fast in throwaway vanilla HTML with Claude Code, then converge inside a design-system playground repo and share a live link instead of Figma specs.
What they did: Caston starts each project with a FigJam board of Mobbin screenshots where he highlights the exact part he likes (so people and agents know what inspired him), plus a project folder with markdown context (merchant pains, requirements) and a vanilla HTML wireframe made with Claude Code. He then opens Shopify's 'playground' (a clone of the admin wired to the real design system and the internal Quick hosting, mock DB and AI proxy), dictates a plan to Claude Code in plan mode on Opus, and gives it three inputs at once: the spoken brief, a screenshot of the wireframe, and the wireframe folder dragged into the terminal. He runs several Claude tabs in parallel on separate concerns (one for visuals, one for a Quick DB for images, one for an LLM integration, plus a variant A/B switcher in the rough prototype), starting with only the core surface before adding scope. He shares with 'dev save', which makes an internal link with built-in comments, and hands PM and engineering the branch commit so they fork and edit the same code; he also built a set of 26 markdown commands for the team (e.g. one that aligns tokens with accessibility or checks empty states).
Results: "what might have taken a few days of effort for a version is now like few hours of effort"; "projects have shrunk from like months to days and weeks"; on a recent project the prototype "has given 80% to the developer", with the remaining 20% being polish and string internationalization; the time spent maintaining a Figma artifact for the end-to-end experience is "down to zero".
Takeaways: Crop and highlight the exact part of a reference screenshot before giving it to a person or an agent; Feed Claude three inputs together: dictated brief, screenshot, and the rough code folder; Start with the main surface only, then add features one at a time so the code stays precise; Run parallel Claude tabs on different concerns, never two on the same code; Prototype AI features in real code with a live LLM, because open-ended conversation can't be designed statically in Figma
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: keep a per-feature folder with a CONTEXT.md (student pains from support/PostHog, requirements) and a throwaway HTML wireframe, then prompt Claude Code in plan mode with brief + screenshot + folder before touching the real React Native screens. Design process: write small markdown slash commands for the team, such as 'check every state' (empty, loading, error) and 'check tokens and contrast', and run them on each prototype. Practice: prototype any AI explanation or doubt-solving feature against a real LLM endpoint rather than static mocks.

Title: How Razorpay Designers use AI to Ship 8 Projects a Month (PJ and Mina)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with PJ and Mina, Razorpay)
Bottom line: Align on how a flow works with ugly Claude artifacts first, then restyle it with the design system MCP, and walk reviews through in the user's voice from a written design doc.
What they did: For every M or L project (2 to 3 weeks or more) Razorpay designers write a design doc (brief, product and business goals, competitive insights, personas, user stories and narrative) and present walkthroughs to their design head in the user's voice ('I am a merchant with a D2C clothing brand, this morning I want to see my orders...') before showing screens, with all feedback written into a thread. PJ uses Figma only for 'visual note taking': a board with a visual audit of the current flow, 1:1 notes, and competitor screenshots from Mobbin, which he shares with Claude as one big visual prompt. Claude then builds functional artifacts (e.g. a 4-step flow vs a long form) that he uses only to align stakeholders on structure; once aligned, he converts to Blade via the design system MCP, giving one Figma screenshot to match the visual language. Small changes skip Figma entirely: PJ codes them and raises a PR, and PMs now send PRDs as markdown files in GitHub PRs. They run agents from Warp with OpenCode and Claude, and dictate long prompts with Whisper.
Results: Designers are expected to close "7 to 8 line items per head in a month" and were given a goal to "raise 10 to 15 PRs this month"; a handoff for a big project "takes about an hour"; a typical problem statement gets "a week" minimum.
Takeaways: Separate 'how it works' alignment (unstyled artifact) from 'how it looks' (design system pass via MCP); Use a Figma board of audit notes, meeting notes and competitor screens as a visual prompt for Claude; Present designs in the user's voice, after the problem and business goal; Have leaders write feedback in a thread so the designer can keep presenting; Run recurring maker sessions, AI open hours and builder days so the team learns tools together
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: in crits, walk through screens as a NEET-PG aspirant ('I'm three months from the exam and opened the app at 6 am to see today's plan') before showing UI, and capture all feedback in one written thread. Today's plan: first build two unstyled Claude artifacts of different structures (e.g. single scrolling list vs stepped sessions) to agree on how it works, then restyle in the real components. Design process: for small copy or spacing fixes, raise the PR directly instead of a Figma handoff.

Title: How Deel Designers Start Prototyping Before PRDs (Chris)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Chris, Deel)
Bottom line: Validate the concept with cheap, deliberately rough prototypes and deep discovery first, and only then spend Claude Code tokens on a high-fidelity prototype in a design-system repo.
What they did: Chris starts some projects from the solution: he builds rough Lovable or Claude Design concepts (e.g. dragging transactions onto invoices vs a fixed transaction with a list of matches for reconciliation), records a 2-minute video for stakeholders and tests with internal users; the side-by-side concept won because it 'prevent[s] more errors'. Deel's engineers built a 'UI playground' repo with many markdown instructions that act as guardrails so Claude only uses the real design system; Chris clones it next to the team's production repo and tells Claude to read the playground rules and implement small changes (a color, a tracking event) as real PRs. He does long discovery in a Figma 'brain dump' (problem context, maps, PRD excerpts) and feeds it to Claude as screenshots for diagrams and plain text for prose to save tokens. When Claude invents a component, he pastes the Storybook link and says 'you are inventing this, please do it correctly with this component'; handoff is a dev-environment link plus a video walkthrough, followed by iterative fixes as engineers find edge cases.
Results: A concept test "takes me like half of a day or... like two hours prompting" and he gets "full validation of the concept... in one day or two days"; Deel has about 90 designers and roughly 4,500 engineers.
Takeaways: Keep concept prototypes visibly rough so people judge the idea, not the polish; Put design-system guardrails in markdown in a shared repo so every designer's Claude prototype uses real components; Don't burn tokens on high-fidelity code before the concept is clear and approved; Feed context as text when it is prose and as screenshots when it is a diagram; Spot invented components by eye and correct Claude with the Storybook link
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: create a shared 'prototype guardrails' markdown (allowed components, tokens, no new primitives) in the OnCourse repo so Claude Code and Cursor prototypes stay on-system, and correct drift by pasting the real component file. Practice: test two rough interaction concepts (e.g. how students review wrong answers) with a few students over a 2-minute video before building the polished version. Design process: hand off with a live build link plus a short video walkthrough instead of static specs.

Title: AI Native Designer shows his Growth Design Process (Clint, Givebutter)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Clint, Givebutter)
Bottom line: Hunt friction weekly by pairing what users say (Enterpret) with what they do (Hex), prototype fast, and ship small A/B/C tests to learn quickly, including that your assumption was wrong.
What they did: Each week Clint pulls nuggets from Granola meeting notes, pastes them into Claude to generate prompts, then runs them in Enterpret with a fixed add-on framework (summarize feedback and patterns, focus on missed opportunities, draft a brainstorm doc by opportunity area with user stories and citations, suggest experiments), and checks behavior via a Hex agent in a shared Slack channel ('talk to data'). He uses Claude Code to invent new things freely (e.g. four CRM onboarding module concepts, each with a built-in state switcher for first visit, partial progress, completed and returning user, plus a 'growth team test' badge) and Magic Patterns, which is wired to Givebutter's Storybook, to refine existing flows on real components. He shares a Loom under 5 minutes in a Slack thread with prototype links, then has Claude send approved screens to a one-Figma-file-per-quarter team file. The team A/B/C tested three ways to ask 'are you switching from another tool?' (dropdown plus yes/no, one-tap options, 'which tool are you coming from').
Results: Tests went "from concept to... working prototype to... ready for deployment" "within 2 days"; only "something like 17%" of users confirmed they were switching in one experiment "and even lower in another", disproving the 'switcher intent' assumption; the 'what tool are you coming from' one-tap variant "tested the best" but "none of them were actually successful"; "we learned within 2 weeks that we were wrong versus... 2 months".
Takeaways: Pair qualitative (what users say) with quantitative (what they do) before choosing a problem; Use a reusable prompt framework when querying feedback tools so outputs are comparable; Build state switchers (first visit, partial, complete, returning) into prototypes so reviewers see every state; Ask onboarding questions as one-tap choices, not dropdown plus confirm; Treat a failed test as a fast lesson about your mental model, not your UI
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: A/B test asking prep stage (e.g. 'which exam and attempt are you preparing for') as one-tap options instead of dropdowns, and check whether the answer really predicts behavior before personalizing on it. Home: prototype a 'getting started' checklist with explicit states (first visit, partial, done, returning 'since you were last here') and a state switcher for review. Design process: run a weekly friction hunt pairing support/review feedback with PostHog funnels, and share findings as a sub-5-minute Loom with prototype links.
